unit.title: Perform basic hair and scalp treatments

summary: This unit teaches you to analyse the hair and scalp, choose a suitable treatment and carry it out safely: protein, moisturising and deep conditioning treatments with a steamer or cap, hot oil treatments, scalp treatments and scalp massage. You will learn the hair and scalp conditions you can treat and those you must refer, how to care for natural, braided and chemically treated hair, how to keep tools and equipment hygienic, and how to give aftercare advice and keep records.

blocks.p: Treatments are the services that look after the hair and scalp between cuts, colours and relaxers: a deep conditioner for dry hair, a protein treatment for weak hair, a hot oil treatment, a scalp treatment for flakes or oiliness, and the scalp massage that goes with them. This unit is for COSMETOLOGY LEVEL 2 trainees. It builds on the shampoo and conditioning unit and the hygiene you already know.

A good treatment starts with a good **analysis**. If you choose the wrong treatment, the hair can get worse: too much protein makes hair hard and brittle, and too much moisture without protein leaves it limp and over-stretchy. You must also know when **not** to treat: cuts, sores, infections and lice mean you stop and refer the client.

blocks.note: How you are assessed: theory papers (multiple-choice questions, short answers and essays) and practical tasks in the Centre's salon: an analysis with a deep conditioning treatment under a steamer, and a scalp massage with a hot oil treatment on natural hair. The assessor watches your consultation, safety checks, timing, client care and clean-up.

blocks.note: If a client says her scalp is burning during a treatment, stop at once. Rinse the product off with plenty of cool water, check the scalp, tell your supervisor, and write it in the accident book. Do not wait to see if it settles.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.note: Jamaica's power supply is 110 V (some heavy equipment 220 V) at 50 Hz. Use equipment made for the Centre's sockets, keep extension cords off wet floors, and never plug in with wet hands. A solar water heater can make the basin water very hot on a sunny afternoon: test it every time.
blocks.label: Jamaica

head: Word
Meaning
rows: Cleaning
Removing hair, dirt and product with detergent and water. Always first, because disinfectant does not work well through dirt.
Disinfecting
Using a chemical, made up and left on for the contact time the label says, to kill most germs on clean tools and surfaces.
Sterilising
Killing all germs and their spores, for example in an autoclave. Used for tools that break the skin.
Single-use
Used once and thrown away: some caps, neck strips, applicator tips.

ul: Wash combs, brushes and clips in warm soapy water, disinfect them for the contact time, dry and store them in a clean, covered container.
Use a fresh towel and gown for every client. Put used ones in a covered laundry bin and wash them hot.
Wipe the chair, basin, trolley, steamer hood and hood dryer with disinfectant between clients.
Wear gloves for products that irritate the skin and for any client with an open spot. Wash your hands before and after each client.
Keep products in their labelled containers, lids closed, in a cool, dry place out of the sun. Use a pump or clean spatula, never your fingers, in a tub.
Read the label, and for chemicals the safety data sheet (SDS), for hazards, storage and first aid.

sections.title: Hair and scalp: structure and analysis

head: Part
What it is
Why it matters for treatments
rows: Follicle
The small pocket in the skin of the scalp that each hair grows from.
Sebaceous glands open into it; infections show here (folliculitis).
Cuticle
The outer layer: overlapping, clear scales.
Smooth cuticle: shine and moisture held in. Raised or damaged cuticle: rough, dull, tangles, loses moisture.
Cortex
The middle layer: keratin (the protein hair is mainly made of) fibres. Gives strength, stretch and colour.
Deep treatments aim to reach it; relaxers and colour work in it.
Medulla
The soft centre; may be missing in fine hair.
Little effect on treatments.

ul: **Sebaceous glands** make **sebum**, the natural oil of the scalp. Too much gives an oily scalp (seborrhoea); too little a dry scalp.
On curly and coily hair, sebum cannot travel easily down the bends, so the lengths are often dry even when the scalp is oily. This is why coily hair needs moisture added.
Healthy hair and skin are slightly acid (about pH 4.5 to 5.5). Conditioners are usually slightly acid so that they help the cuticle lie smooth and flat.

flow: Ask about hair care, products and chemical services
Ask how the scalp feels: itching, flaking, tightness, soreness
Look at and feel the hair in good light
Test porosity
Test elasticity
Note texture, density and curl pattern
Part the hair and check the whole scalp
Record and choose the treatment

head: Check
How you do it
What the result tells you
rows: Porosity
Slide your finger and thumb along a dry strand from the ends towards the scalp, and watch how fast it takes up water.
Smooth, water beads on it: low porosity (tight cuticle); slow to take in products
Slightly rough: normal
Very rough, soaks up water at once, dries fast: high porosity (raised or damaged cuticle); needs moisture and a smoothing treatment
Elasticity
Gently stretch one wet strand held at both ends.
Stretches and springs back: good
Snaps after very little stretch: dry and brittle; needs moisture
Stretches a long way, does not spring back, feels gummy or mushy: weak; needs protein
Texture
Feel a single hair: fine, medium or coarse.
Fine hair is weighed down by heavy products; coarse hair takes longer to take in products.
Density
Part the hair and see how much scalp shows: low, medium, high.
High density needs more product, smaller sections and more time.
Curl pattern
Look at clean hair: straight, wavy, curly, coily.
The tighter the curl, the drier and more fragile the lengths.
Condition
Look, feel and ask about history.
Normal, dry, oily, damaged or chemically treated: guides the products.

blocks.note: Texture and density are not the same. A client who says her hair is 'thick' may have a great many fine hairs: fine texture, high density. Record both.
blocks.label: Tip

ul: 'Does your scalp itch, flake or feel tight?' (dry scalp, dandruff or product build-up)
'What do you use on your hair and scalp at home, and how often do you wash?'
'Have you had a relaxer, colour or smoothing treatment, and when?'
'Do you use heat tools? How often?'
'Are you allergic to anything, or have you had a reaction to a product?'
'What would you like your hair to be like?'

blocks.p: A **contra-indication** is anything that means a treatment should not go ahead, or must be changed. Part the hair in several places and check the whole scalp, especially the nape and behind the ears, before any treatment or massage. A **contagious** (infectious) condition can pass from person to person: you stop and refer.

head: Condition
What you see
Contagious?
What you do
rows: Dandruff (pityriasis capitis)
Small white or greyish flakes on the scalp and shoulders; may itch; no redness or sores.
No
Treat: anti-dandruff shampoo and scalp treatment as the maker says; regular washing. Refer if red, sore or not improving.
Dry scalp
Fine, dry flakes; tight, itchy feeling; no redness.
No
Treat: gentle moisturising shampoo; moisturising scalp treatment or light oil.
Oily scalp (seborrhoea)
Greasy shine; hair goes limp soon after washing; flakes may be yellowish and stick to the scalp.
No
Treat: gentle balancing shampoo; light massage only, because firm massage can increase oil flow; warm, not hot, water.
Product build-up
Dull, heavy hair; white residue; itch.
No
Clarifying shampoo; light conditioner afterwards.
Traction alopecia
Thinning or bald patches at the edges from tight styles.
No
Treat gently, no pulling; advise looser styles; see a doctor if it does not improve.
Psoriasis or eczema
Psoriasis: thick silvery scales on red patches. Eczema: red, dry, itchy skin that may crack.
No
If unbroken, mild products and light touch. If broken, bleeding or inflamed, do not treat; refer.
Head lice (pediculosis capitis)
Insects; oval eggs (nits) glued to the hair near the scalp at the nape and behind the ears; itching.
Yes
Do not treat. Tell the client kindly in private; suggest a pharmacist or doctor; disinfect tools; bag towels for a hot wash.
Ringworm (tinea capitis)
Round, scaly patches; broken hairs; bald patches. A fungal infection.
Yes
Do not treat. Refer to a doctor.
Impetigo
Weeping sores with honey-coloured crusts. A bacterial infection.
Yes
Do not treat. Refer to a doctor.
Boils or folliculitis
Red, painful lumps or pus spots at the follicles.
Can spread
Do not work over them; refer.
Cuts, sores, grazes, recent stitches
Broken skin.
No, but germs can enter
No massage and no products over the area; postpone or refer.

blocks.note: You are not a doctor. Do not tell the client she has a disease, and do not try to treat an infection or infestation. Describe what you saw, in private and kindly, explain why the treatment cannot go ahead today, and advise her to see a doctor or pharmacist. Record it, and clean and disinfect everything she touched.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.note: Head lice spread easily among children and are no sign of a dirty home. Speak kindly and privately to the parent, never in front of other clients or the child's friends.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.h: Other things that stop or change a treatment

ul: A known **allergy** to an oil, nut, fragrance or other ingredient: read the label and choose a different product.
A **chemical service next** (relaxer, colour, perm): keep massage light with no scratching or firm friction, and follow the maker's instructions about whether the scalp should be washed beforehand.
A client with **neck problems, dizziness or high or low blood pressure**: use a front-wash basin or extra support, keep heat short, and stop if she feels unwell.
**Recent surgery**, **pregnancy** or a client under medical treatment: ask, and refer to her doctor if you are unsure.

blocks.p: Scalp massage loosens dirt and dead skin, increases the blood flow to the scalp, spreads products evenly and relaxes the client. Always use the **pads of the fingers**, never the nails, with an even rhythm and pressure.

head: Movement
How you do it
When you use it
rows: Effleurage
Light, slow, smooth stroking with the palms or flat of the fingers.
To begin and end a massage and link movements; to spread product. Soothing.
Petrissage
Slow, firm kneading: the finger pads press and lift the scalp, moving it over the bone beneath.
The deeper movement in a treatment massage. Relaxes and helps products work in.
Friction
Small circles or brisk rubbing with the finger pads, moving the scalp over the bone.
To stimulate the scalp and lift dirt and dead skin. Use lightly or leave out on a tender scalp or before a chemical service.

blocks.h: A scalp massage step by step

flow: Check for contra-indications; gown the client and make sure she is comfortable; short nails and clean hands
Apply a scalp product or oil if the treatment needs one
Begin with effleurage from the front hairline back to the nape
Use petrissage and friction in an even pattern over the whole scalp: front, sides, crown and nape
Keep a steady rhythm and even pressure; ask if the pressure is right
Finish with slow effleurage
Carry on with the treatment or the shampoo

head: Situation
What to do
rows: Oily scalp
Keep it gentle: firm massage can increase oil flow.
Dry or sensitive scalp
Light pressure and a rich product; shorter time.
Open cuts or sores; infection
No massage.
Before a relaxer or colour
Light only: it can irritate the scalp so the chemical stings or burns.
Thinning hair or traction alopecia
Gentle pressure; do not tug.
Braids, locs and weaves
Press and pat the scalp along the parts; do not rub.
Client asks for less pressure, has a headache or neck pain
Do as she asks; stop if she feels unwell.

blocks.note: Nails scratch the scalp. Scratches sting, let germs in and make chemical services burn.
blocks.label: Safety

sections.title: Treatment products and how they work

blocks.p: Hair needs both protein (strength) and moisture (softness and stretch). Use the elasticity test and the feel of the hair to choose.

head: What you find
What it usually means
Choose
rows: Dry, rough, hard, brittle; snaps after very little stretch
Lacking moisture
A moisturising deep conditioning treatment
Limp, mushy or gummy when wet; stretches a long way and does not spring back
Weak: lacking protein
A protein treatment, then moisture
Stiff and brittle after many protein treatments
Too much protein
Stop protein for now; use moisturising treatments
Healthy feel; good stretch and spring-back
Balanced
Regular conditioning to keep it so

ul: **Protein treatment:** puts protein back into hair that has lost strength; for weak, over-processed or over-stretchy hair (after relaxers, colour, lots of heat). Use only as the maker says; **too many protein treatments make the hair stiff, dry and easy to break**.
**Moisturising treatment:** adds water and softening oils; for dry, dull, rough or brittle hair that still has good elasticity (common in coily natural hair).
Too much moisture and too little protein leaves hair limp and over-soft, so it stretches and breaks. That is why many protein treatments are followed by a moisturising conditioner.
The balance changes after colour, relaxers, heat and sun: test every visit.

head: Treatment
What it does
For
Time and heat
rows: Deep (penetrating) conditioner
Rich product whose small molecules pass through a lifted cuticle into the cortex.
Dry, porous, damaged or treated hair
Often 10 to 30 minutes, usually with heat; as the maker says.
Protein treatment
Strengthens weak hair for a time.
Weak, limp, over-stretchy hair
As the maker says; only now and then.
Moisturising treatment
Restores water and softness.
Dry, brittle hair
Regularly, as needed; heat helps.
Hot oil treatment
Warm oil softens dry hair and scalp.
Dry hair and scalp
Warm, not hot; covered for the maker's time.
Scalp treatment
Product for a dry, oily or flaky scalp.
Specific scalp need
As the label says.
Clarifying shampoo
Removes product, oil and mineral build-up.
Build-up; before some treatments
Not every wash; condition after.
Leave-in conditioner
Stays in to soften, detangle and protect.
Dry, curly, coily and treated hair
Not rinsed out.

blocks.note: Always follow the manufacturer's instructions for amount, time and heat. If the label and your habit disagree, the label wins; if unsure, ask your instructor.
blocks.label: Tip

ul: Gentle heat lifts the cuticle a little and speeds the product, so more of it gets into the hair.
A **plastic (processing) cap** holds in warmth and moisture, stops the treatment drying on the hair and keeps the client clean.
Too much heat or too long can irritate or burn the scalp and dry the hair. Not every treatment uses heat: read the label.

head: Equipment
Type of heat
Check before and after
rows: Steamer
Moist heat (steam)
Cable and plug undamaged; hands dry
The kind of water the maker says (many say distilled water), filled to the right line
Hood at the distance the maker gives; keep steam away from the face
Emptied, cleaned and descaled as the maker says
Hood dryer
Dry heat
Clean; cable and plug undamaged
Low to medium heat, as the maker says
Hood over the plastic cap; client comfortable
Heat cap (thermal cap)
Dry heat from a cap over the plastic cap
Cap and cable undamaged; heat set as the maker says
Plastic cap and warm towel
Body heat held in
No electricity needed; use when no steamer is available

blocks.h: Deep conditioning treatment with a steamer

flow: Consult, analyse the hair and scalp, check contra-indications, choose and agree the treatment
Clean and disinfect the station; check the steamer: cable, plug, correct water and level; dry hands
Gown the client with a fresh towel
Shampoo the hair; squeeze and blot out the extra water
Divide the hair into sections
Apply the deep conditioner section by section, from roots to ends (or mid-lengths to ends if the maker says), and comb through gently with a wide-tooth comb
Cover with a plastic cap and place the steamer hood as the maker says; switch on and set a timer for the maker's time
Stay nearby; check she is comfortable and not too hot; keep steam away from her face
When the time is up, switch off and move the steamer away
Rinse with comfortably warm water until clean, finishing cool; blot, and finish with low to medium heat
Advise, clean the steamer as the maker says, and record

blocks.note: Write down the time as soon as the client goes under the heat. Example: treatment on at 2:40 p.m., maker says 15 minutes, so rinse at 2:55 p.m. Always use the time on the product, not a guess.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.note: Never leave a client alone under a steamer or dryer. Check every few minutes and ask if she is comfortable. Switch off and move the equipment away at once if she feels too hot, faint or unwell.
blocks.label: Safety

flow: Consult; check the scalp for cuts, sores or infection; ask about allergies to oils or nuts
Gown the client and protect her clothes with a fresh towel
Warm the oil as the maker says, for example by standing the bottle in a bowl of warm water; never over a flame or on a hot tool
Test a drop on the inside of your wrist: it should be only comfortably warm
Part the hair into sections; apply the oil to the scalp and along the hair with an applicator bottle or fingers
Give a gentle scalp massage with effleurage and friction
Cover with a plastic cap and warm towel, or sit under a warm dryer, for the maker's time
Shampoo the oil out well and condition
Wipe up any oil at once: it makes floors slippery

ul: Hot oil softens dry hair and a dry scalp. On an oily scalp, apply the oil to the lengths only.
Warm oil, not hot: heated oil can burn the scalp. Water heated to a safe comfortable temperature in a bowl is the safest way.

head: Scalp
Treatment
Notes
rows: Dandruff
Anti-dandruff shampoo and scalp treatment, left on for the time on the label
Does not treat infections: refer those.
Dry scalp
Moisturising shampoo; light scalp oil or moisturising treatment; gentle massage
Water not too hot.
Oily scalp
Shampoo for oily hair; balancing scalp treatment; light massage
Conditioner on the ends only; no heavy grease.
Build-up
Clarifying shampoo, then conditioner
Not every wash.

blocks.h: Applying a deep conditioner to thick hair

ul: Divide into sections and clip them. Work through each section, applying from the roots to the ends (as the maker says) and combing through with a wide-tooth comb.
Thick or high-density hair needs more time, more product and smaller sections so every strand is coated.
Leave on for the time on the maker's instructions: too short does not work; too long can leave hair hard (protein) or limp (moisture).
Rinse until water runs clear and the hair no longer feels slippery, checking the nape, behind the ears and the hairline. Use comfortably warm water, checked on your wrist and with the client.
Blot with a clean towel; do not rub. Wet hair is weaker and stretches easily.
Dry fragile hair gently: a towel blot and low to medium heat, with a heat protectant.
Help the client sit up slowly; some feel light-headed after leaning back.

sections.title: Natural, braided and chemically treated hair

ul: Every bend in a coil is a weak point; sebum cannot travel down it easily, so the lengths are dry. Coily hair breaks easily when handled roughly.
**Detangle with conditioner**, using your fingers or a wide-tooth comb, **from the ends up**, in small sections. Combing from the roots pushes knots into bigger tangles.
Use a moisturising, often sulphate-free, shampoo or a co-wash; a moisturising deep treatment; then a **leave-in conditioner**, sealed with a light oil or cream.
Keep the hair stretched and protected: loose twists or plaits, and a satin bonnet or scarf at night.
Low manipulation: fewer combings, gentle handling, protective styles.
Cleanse the scalp between the braids: put diluted shampoo in an **applicator bottle** and apply along the parts. Press and pat; do not rub the braids.
Rinse very well; shampoo left behind causes itching and flakes. Use a light scalp product on the parts; heavy creams and waxes build up.
Squeeze out the water, blot, and **dry fully** under a hood dryer if needed. Damp braids can smell of mildew.
Do not keep braids in too long (many stylists advise about 6 to 8 weeks).

blocks.p: **Traction alopecia** is hair loss caused by styles that pull the hair too tightly: tight braids, weaves, ponytails. Signs: thinning or bald patches at the hairline or edges, small bumps, soreness. Treat the scalp gently with no pulling; advise looser styles and breaks between tight styles; suggest a doctor if it is severe or does not improve.

blocks.note: A client who has braided hair pulled tight at the hairline and is losing hair at the edges needs honest advice: choose looser styles, and see a doctor if it does not improve. Do not apply tension to the edges in your own styling.
blocks.label: Tip

ul: Relaxed hair is weaker and more porous; the line where new growth meets relaxed hair is the weakest point. Detangle from the ends, hold the hair above the line, and balance moisture and protein.
Coloured and lightened hair fades and dries when the cuticle lifts: use colour-care, sulphate-free, acid-balanced products, lukewarm water and a cool final rinse.
After a chemical service, follow the maker's advice on when the hair may be washed and treated.

blocks.note: Many clients wear locs for religious or cultural reasons, for example as members of the Rastafari faith. Ask how she wants the locs treated and which products she will accept, and respect her wishes. Use residue-free products and dry locs right through.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.note: Sun, sea and swimming pools dry the hair and fade colour. Advise clients to rinse with fresh water and apply a leave-in before and after swimming, and to cover the hair in strong sun.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.p: Tell the client what the treatment did and how to keep the result. Base the advice on what you found, give the reason, and keep it simple.

head: Client
Advice
Why
rows: Dry natural hair
Moisturise regularly; leave-in conditioner
Detangle only when damp and conditioned
Satin scarf or pillowcase at night; loose protective styles
Keeps moisture in and cuts breakage.
Weak or over-processed hair
Protein and moisture in balance
Less heat, with a heat protectant
Gentle handling
Strengthens without making the hair stiff.
Oily scalp
Shampoo for oily hair; warm, not hot, water
No heavy grease on the scalp
Controls oil without irritation.
Dandruff
Anti-dandruff shampoo for the label's time
See a doctor if red, sore or no better
Controls flaking; more needs medical advice.
Braids
Wash the scalp with diluted shampoo; dry fully
Light products; take braids out in time
Prevents build-up, mildew and tension.

ul: Advise her to avoid very hot water, harsh shampoo, high heat and tight styles, and to protect hair from sun and sea water.
Tell her to contact the salon if the scalp itches or becomes sore after a treatment.
Recommend a course of treatments or the next visit, and suggest suitable products, honestly and without pressure. Know the prices in J$.

flow: Put on gloves; clear hair from the basin and drain
Clean the basin, chair and trolley with detergent and water, then disinfect for the contact time
Empty, wipe and dry the steamer; clean the hood dryer as the maker says
Put used towels and gowns in the closed laundry bin
Clean then disinfect combs, brushes and clips
Put lids on products and return them; wipe bottles
Wipe up all oil and water; leave a wet floor sign until dry
Wash and dry your hands

head: What to record
Example
rows: Date, name and contact details
07/11/2026, Camille Bryan, Old Harbour
Analysis and test results
Natural, coily; medium texture, high density; high porosity; snaps when stretched
Scalp and contra-indications
Dry; no sores, lice or infection
Treatment, products, heat and time
Moisturising deep conditioner; steamer, 20 minutes as the maker says
Result, reactions or problems
Soft, easy to detangle; no reaction
Advice and next visit
Leave-in; satin bonnet; treatment again in 2 weeks
Stylist
A. Clarke (trainee), checked by the instructor

blocks.p: Records show what works for that client, help any stylist plan the next visit and protect the client and the salon if there is a complaint or reaction.

blocks.note: Client records are personal information, kept private and secure under Jamaica's Data Protection Act. Never discuss one client's hair or scalp with another.
blocks.label: Jamaica

ul: I can check steamers, dryers and cables before use, and never leave a client under heat.
I can warm oil safely, test it on my inner wrist and apply it without burning the scalp.
I can clean then disinfect tools and equipment, and explain the difference between disinfecting and sterilising.
I can describe the cuticle, cortex, medulla and follicle, and say where sebum comes from.
I can test porosity and elasticity and note texture, density and curl pattern.
I can choose between a protein and a moisturising treatment, and say what too much protein does.
I can recognise dandruff, dry scalp, oily scalp, psoriasis, lice, ringworm, impetigo and cuts, and say which are contagious and which I refer.
I can describe effleurage, petrissage and friction, and give a scalp massage step by step.
I can adjust massage for an oily or tender scalp, before a chemical service, and over braids.
I can give a deep conditioning treatment with a steamer, timed as the maker says.
I can give a hot oil treatment safely.
I can care for natural, braided, relaxed and coloured hair and spot traction alopecia.
I can give aftercare advice, clean up and fill in a record card.

blocks.note: In essay answers, give the reason for each step. For example: 'I test a drop of warm oil on my inner wrist, so that I do not burn the client's scalp.'
blocks.label: Tip

A contagious bacterial skin infection with weeping, honey-coloured crusts.

Hair loss from styles that pull the hair too tightly.

Slow, firm kneading that lifts and presses the scalp.
Small circles or brisk rubbing with the finger pads.
A treatment that strengthens weak, over-stretchy hair.
A treatment that restores water and softness to dry hair.
A rich treatment that passes into the cortex, usually with heat.
A treatment in which warm oil is worked into the scalp and hair.
A conditioner left in after the final rinse.
A shampoo that removes product, oil and mineral build-up.

The client's record of analysis, treatment, products, timing, advice and reactions.

c1.title: A dry, brittle head in Old Harbour
c1.text: Camille Bryan, 27, comes to a salon in Old Harbour for a treatment. Her hair is natural and tightly coiled; it feels hard and rough and her ends are dry. When trainee Jodi stretches a single wet strand, it snaps after only a little stretch. When she slides her fingers along a dry strand towards the scalp it feels very rough, and water sprayed on it soaks in almost at once. Camille uses a lot of protein products at home because she was told they make hair strong.

c2.title: The steamer and a lunch-hour rush in Savanna-la-Mar
c2.text: A trainee, Marlon, gives Sandra a deep conditioning treatment under a steamer at a salon in Savanna-la-Mar. The maker says 20 minutes. As the steamer warms up, he notices the water tank is filled with tap water, the cable has a cracked outer cover and his hands are wet. A client waiting for the next chair is complaining about the delay. After starting the timer, Marlon steps out to take a phone call.

c3.title: A hot oil treatment in Montego Bay
c3.text: At a salon in Montego Bay, trainee Chantel is giving Mrs Dorothy Gray a hot oil treatment. Mrs Gray's scalp is dry and tight, with fine flakes, and she mentions an allergy to peanuts. The oil in the bottle is labelled as coconut oil. Chantel is tempted to heat it in a small pot over a flame to save time, and to check it by dipping a finger in. Some oil drips on the floor beside the chair.

c4.title: A scalp in Falmouth
c4.text: Nicole, 9, is brought by her mother to a salon in Falmouth for a scalp treatment and a wash. While parting the hair, trainee Kemar sees tiny whitish specks stuck to the hairs close to the scalp behind the ears. Nicole keeps scratching. In the same salon, an older client, Mr Hugh Smith, has an oily scalp and asks for a firm, stimulating massage because 'it feels good'. Another client, Ms Pauline Reid, wears tight box braids and has thin patches at her hairline.

questions.q: What do Jodi's tests show about Camille's hair?
o: High porosity and dry, brittle hair that lacks moisture
Low porosity and strong hair that has too much moisture
High porosity and weak hair that lacks protein
Normal porosity and healthy hair that needs only a trim
questions.why: A rough feel and water soaking in at once show a raised cuticle: high porosity. A strand that snaps after little stretch is dry and brittle and needs moisture. Gummy, over-stretchy hair is the kind that lacks protein.

questions.q: Which treatment should Jodi choose first?
o: A protein treatment, to strengthen it quickly and add some stiffness
A clarifying shampoo followed by a hot comb to smooth it out
A moisturising deep conditioning treatment, with a steamer or cap
A relaxer touch-up, to make the hair easier to manage at home
questions.why: Dry, rough, brittle hair that snaps needs moisture. A moisturising deep treatment with heat helps it take in water. More protein would make it stiffer, and heat or chemicals would damage it further.

questions.q: Camille uses protein products at home all the time. What is the likely effect on her hair?
o: It makes the hair limp, soft and mushy so that it hangs down
It makes the hair stiff and hard, so that it breaks easily
It lifts the cuticle and makes the hair grow faster each month
It has no effect on the hair once the hair has become wet
questions.why: Too much protein leaves hair stiff, dry and brittle. Protein is for weak, over-stretchy hair, and only now and then, as the maker says; the balance with moisture matters.

questions.q: After rinsing the treatment, how should Jodi finish Camille's hair to keep the moisture in?
o: Apply a leave-in, seal with a light oil or cream, and put in loose twists
Blow-dry it straight on the highest heat, to close the cuticle quickly
Pull it into a tight bun with a thick rubber band while it is still wet
Leave it wet and uncovered so the sun can dry it naturally outdoors
questions.why: A leave-in conditioner sealed with a light oil or cream holds moisture in, and loose twists keep the coils stretched and protected. High heat, tight bands and wet hair left in the sun dry and break coily hair.

questions.q: Before starting the treatment, which fault should Marlon deal with first?
o: The waiting client, because every minute of delay costs the salon money
The cracked cable and his wet hands, because of the risk of shock
The tap water, because it is not as clean as bottled water would be
The timer, because it has been set up in the wrong place on the trolley
questions.why: A damaged cable and wet hands together can cause an electric shock. A damaged item is taken out of use and reported, and hands are dried before touching plugs. The water type matters too, but safety comes first.

questions.q: What water should Marlon put in the steamer?
o: Tap water, since it is the cleanest water that the salon has
Water mixed with a little shampoo, to cleanse the hair as it steams
Salt water, since it is said to carry the heat better than fresh
Whatever the maker's instructions say, often distilled water
questions.why: Follow the maker's instructions: many say distilled water, because hard water leaves scale that blocks the steamer. Never add products to the water.

questions.q: What should Marlon have done after starting the timer?
o: Stayed close, checked Sandra's comfort and watched the time
Left her for the full 20 minutes so the steam could work
Raised the heat so the treatment would finish sooner
Asked another client to watch her while he took the call
questions.why: A client under heat must never be left. Stay close, check every few minutes, keep steam away from her face, and be ready to switch off if she feels too hot or faint.

questions.q: When the 20 minutes are up, what should Marlon do first?
o: Lift the hood and leave the steamer running while he rinses her hair
Switch off and move the steamer away, then rinse with warm water
Rinse with cold water at once, because it closes the cuticle quickly
Rub the hair dry with a towel before rinsing it out at the basin
questions.why: Switch off and move the equipment away first, so no one is burned by hot steam or trips on a running machine. Then rinse until clean with comfortably warm water, finishing cool.

questions.q: How should Chantel warm the oil safely?
o: In a small pot over a flame, stirred until it smells warm enough to use
In the microwave until it starts to bubble around the edges of the bottle
As the maker says, such as standing the bottle in a bowl of warm water
On the hot plate of the hood dryer, to save time in a busy salon
questions.why: Oil must never be heated over a flame or on a hot tool: it can burn the scalp and start a fire. Standing the bottle in warm water warms it gently and safely.

questions.q: How should Chantel check that the oil is safe to apply?
o: Dip a finger into the bottle to feel its heat
Test a drop on the inside of her wrist
Smell it to see whether it is still fresh
Ask Mrs Gray whether it feels warm after it is on her scalp
questions.why: The inside of the wrist is sensitive, like the scalp. Test a drop on it before the oil touches the client. Dipping a finger in the bottle puts germs in the oil, and waiting until it is on the scalp is too late.

questions.q: Mrs Gray told Chantel about an allergy to peanuts. What should Chantel do before using the oil?
o: Use the oil, since coconut is not a peanut and cannot cause a problem
Read the label and choose another oil if there is any doubt
Apply a small amount to her arm and wait ten minutes before starting
Ask Mrs Gray to sign a form saying that she accepts the risk
questions.why: Ask about allergies and read the label for any ingredient she may react to. If you are unsure, choose a different product. Signing a form does not make an unsafe treatment safe.

questions.q: Oil has dripped on the floor beside the chair. What should Chantel do?
o: Wipe it up at once and put out a wet floor sign until it is dry
Leave it until the treatment is finished, since oil dries by itself
Cover it with a towel so that nobody steps in it
Tell Mrs Gray to be careful when she stands up
questions.why: Oil makes floors very slippery. Wipe it up at once and warn people with a sign until the floor is dry. A towel left on the floor is a slip hazard of its own.

questions.q: What are the whitish specks Kemar has found most likely to be?
o: Dandruff flakes from a dry, itchy scalp
Dried product left over from the last wash
Head lice eggs (nits) glued to the hairs
Scales of skin from a patch of psoriasis
questions.why: Nits are glued to the hair close to the scalp, often behind the ears and at the nape, and do not brush off. Dandruff and dried product flake off easily, and psoriasis scales sit on the skin.

questions.q: What should Kemar do next?
o: Give Nicole an anti-dandruff treatment and a gentle scalp massage to help the itch
Stop, tell her mother kindly in private, and suggest a pharmacist or doctor
Carry on with the treatment as booked, but use a fresh towel and gown for her
Comb out the eggs himself with a fine comb and then go on and give the treatment
questions.why: Head lice are contagious, so the treatment does not go ahead. A stylist does not treat an infestation: tell the parent privately and kindly, and suggest a pharmacist or doctor. Then clean and disinfect the tools and bag the towels for a hot wash.

questions.q: Mr Smith wants a firm, stimulating massage for his oily scalp. What should the trainee advise?
o: A firm massage is best, since it clears the pores of excess oil
A firm massage with hot water to break down the grease on the scalp
A gentle massage, because firm massage can increase the flow of oil
No massage at all, because an oily scalp can spread to other clients
questions.why: Firm massage and hot water can make the sebaceous glands produce more oil. Keep the massage gentle and the water warm, not hot. An oily scalp is not contagious.

questions.q: What is the most likely cause of the thin patches at the hairline of Ms Reid, who wears tight box braids?
o: Ringworm, which spreads along the hairline from other clients
Dandruff, which blocks the follicles with flakes
Too many protein treatments, which make the hair break at the roots
Traction alopecia, from the braids pulling on the hair
questions.why: Thinning at the hairline or edges where braids, weaves or ponytails pull tightly is traction alopecia. Ringworm leaves round scaly patches, and dandruff and protein do not cause patches at the edges.

questions.q: How should Ms Reid's scalp be cleansed between her braids?
o: Rub strong shampoo firmly into the whole length of every braid to lift the dirt
Leave the scalp alone until the braids have been taken out at the next visit
Use diluted shampoo in an applicator bottle along the parts, pressing gently
Soak the braids in clarifying shampoo for ten minutes before rinsing them well
questions.why: Diluted shampoo along the parts reaches the scalp without frizzing or loosening the braids. Press and pat, rinse very well, and dry fully, since damp braids can smell of mildew.

questions.q: Why must a comb be washed before it is put into disinfectant?
o: Soap mixes with the disinfectant and makes it stronger
Disinfectant cannot work properly through hair and dirt
The comb would rust if it went in without being washed
Disinfectant only works on tools that are already wet
questions.why: Cleaning always comes first: hair, grease and product shield germs from the disinfectant. Then the tool is disinfected for the contact time on the label.

questions.q: A client has mild, unbroken patches of eczema on her scalp and asks for a treatment. What is the best response?
o: Refuse, because eczema is contagious and could spread to the stylist
Use mild products and a light touch, and avoid any broken skin
Use a firm massage to loosen and lift off the scales of skin
Apply a hot oil treatment and leave it on longer than usual
questions.why: Eczema is not contagious. If the skin is unbroken, work gently with mild products; if it is broken, bleeding or very inflamed, do not treat and suggest a doctor.

questions.q: The maker says a deep conditioner must stay on for 15 minutes under heat. The cap goes on and the timer starts at 3:10 p.m. When should the stylist rinse?
o: At 3:20 p.m.
At 3:25 p.m.
At 3:30 p.m.
At 3:40 p.m.
questions.why: 3:10 p.m. plus 15 minutes is 3:25 p.m. Always use the time on the maker's instructions, write it down or set a timer, and stay with the client.
